page_title: The productivity tax you pay for context switching

sources.entry: How Context Switching Sabotages Your Productivity

summary.title: The productivity tax you pay for context switching
summary.one_liner: Context switching drains focus through attention residue and cognitive costs, and you can reduce it with batching, time blocking, distraction audits, and asynchronous communication.
takeaways: Each interruption leaves attention residue that lowers performance on the next task, and returning to a task can take up to 23 minutes to refocus.
Capture tasks outside your head and use a framework such as the Eisenhower matrix to decide what to focus on.
Reduce switches by batching similar tasks, time blocking, time boxing, or using the Pomodoro method (25 minutes of work, 5-minute break).
Run a distraction audit for a week to find triggers, then turn off notifications, close unused apps, and limit tabs.
Set team norms for asynchronous communication and limit how often you check email to reduce always-on pressure.
summary.summary: This Doist blog article by Elaine Meyer explains what context switching is, drawing on computing history and research on attention residue, working memory, and the dopamine-driven pull of notifications. It describes the costs of switching, including lost productivity, reduced cognitive function, depleted energy, and misplaced priorities. The second half offers nine practical strategies, such as capturing tasks, prioritizing with frameworks, batching and time blocking, screen-free breaks, distraction logs, and asynchronous communication. It is written as a guide with cited studies and includes a promotional note for Doist's Twist app.
